On the occasion of the opening of the summer retreat, he ascends the hall and cites the case of Chan Master Tianping Yi, who once went to Xiyuan.
He used to say of himself, "Let alone understanding the Buddha-dharma; nowadays, one cannot even find a person capable of raising a kōan. One day, Xiyuan encountered him and said:
The Master called for Yunchong Yi. Yi raised his head; the Master said, "Wrong. Yi walked two or three steps; the Master again said, "Wrong. Yi approached him;
the Master said, "Those two 'wrongs' just now—was it West Hall that was wrong, or was it you, the Senior Monk?
Yi said, "It was I who was wrong. The Master said, "Wrong, wrong! Yi then withdrew. The Master said, "Stay here for the summer retreat; I wish to deliberate with you, Senior Monk."
"To deliberate is to be doubly mistaken. At that time, Yì simply acted. After he took up residence at the monastery, he said to the assembly:
"When I first set out on my travels as a pilgrim, I was blown by the winds of karma to the place of the Elder Sīmíng in Rùzhōu. There, I was subjected to two consecutive 'mistakes.'"
[The Master] further detained him for the summer retreat, saying, "Wait until we can deliberate together. I do not say that it was a mistake at that time;
I knew it was a mistake long before we set out for the South. The Master said, "Detaining a monk for the summer retreat is an ordinary matter, yet to deliberate twice over it is truly extraordinary.
How many times has the mulberry field turned into the blue sea? From the beginning, painted cakes have never satisfied hunger."
Ascending the hall on the Emperor’s Birthday: Auspicious omens appear in the River and Luo; a Sage has arisen. Ten thousand nations sing and chant, all imbued with the Supreme Transformation;
the eight reaches of the world offer tribute, together rejoicing in peace and prosperity. For the patch-robed monks beneath the forest trees, there is a share in this gratitude.
With one strike of the pure sounding-stone and one invocation of the Buddha’s name, we pray that our Sovereign may enjoy ten million springs.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Once, while the Great Master Mazu was enjoying the moon with Baizhang, Nanquan, and Xitang, the Master asked, “At this very moment, what is it?
Xitang replied, “It is precisely right for making offerings. Baizhang said, “It is precisely right for practicing cultivation.
Nanquan shook his sleeves and departed. The Master remarked, “The Sutras return to the Tripitaka; Zen returns to the sea. Only Puhua...”
"I wish to transcend the mundane world alone. The Master said, "In the monastic communities, many take 'diao' for 'dao' and confuse 'yu' with 'lu.
You discuss the three great beings’ discourse on playing with the moon, yet you fail to realize that Mazu Daoshi’s nostrils have lost one half."
Ascending the hall: Yesterday, I went outside the city walls to receive the Imperial Incense.
I heard the conversation between two families. One family said, "If you do not know the price of traveling east, how can you expect the buying and selling to be equal?
The other family said, "Riding a horse is not as good as sailing a boat; how can coming and going be comparable? [The Master] picked up [the whisk].
The Master said: "Cast-iron Kunlun performs the *zhazhi* dance; it makes Old Man Wang of East Village fall over with laughter.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked: "Not valuing one's own numinous spirit, one seeks liberation; for whom do you transmit the news of coming and going? The Master said:
The blind man shouts at the thief-tiger. Xuefeng said, "Once a word has been uttered, even four horses cannot overtake it. Xuedou said, "A sharp and clever monk;
he possesses it naturally. Xuefeng said, "Onlookers laugh. Xuedou said, "A beggar sees only small profit. Xuefeng said, [Silence]. Xuedou said, [Silence].
"Accustomed to passing before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, holding a golden spear in hand to celebrate the Great Peace. The Master said, "Keep this clearly in mind," and then continued:

"One Sudhana at the Huayan assembly, one Dragon Girl at the Lotus Sutra assembly, and one butcher at the Nirvana assembly—these are all the very models of those who attain Buddhahood on the spot. After a long silence, he said: "The sweet melon reaches [to its core]..."

The stem is sweet; the bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip. This land and the Western Heaven are a hundred thousand leagues apart. From the winter solstice to Cold Food Festival is one hundred and five days.
[He] ascended the hall and cited an ancient master’s verse, saying: "Repeatedly calling for you to return home, yet you cling to the flawless white jade. Greedily toward...
Dust and sand are scattered before the gate; withered trees sprout new buds. Every year, in the second and third months, ants devour raw iron, and peonies bloom everywhere throughout the city.
A turtle bites a shrimp. [The Master] strikes his whisk and descends from the seat.
The Small General Talk for the End of the Summer Retreat: The entire world of the ten directions is the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment;
the entire world of the ten directions is the true eye of Maheśvara. You all, during these ninety days, when you straighten your spine and sit upright—
When burning incense and prostrating before the Buddha while reciting sutras; when observing various phenomena such as pagodas and marketplaces;

when hearing various sounds such as those of bells, chimes, gongs, and drums; and even during all manner of activities—picking up the spoon, setting down the chopsticks, speaking or remaining silent, moving or staying still—if you can see through these directly and intimately, then there is no Śākyamuni before you and no Maitreya behind you.

Le! To cast the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters, and to contain Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed—here, even the waxen man from the Western Heaven and the iron pellet from this Eastern Land are of no use at all.
If you have not yet reached this state, then teams of unperforated iron hammers will run about;
how lamentable that the lineage of Shaolin would be extinguished! Again, it is said that when the Great Master Yunmen was at the end of summer, he questioned a monk:

[The Master] said: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, without touching upon the ordinary, bring me a phrase of the Way. A monk had no reply. [The Master] spoke on his behalf, saying: "The third of the month, the eleventh;
the middle ninth, the seventh of the waning phase. The Master said: "Everyone says that Master Yunmen was selling jewels and happened to bump into a blind Persian.
Little do they know that, without cause, he spoke of 'the third and the eleventh, the middle ninth and the seventh,' which has cracked people's laughter."
[The Master] struck the whisk and descended from the seat.
Entering the hall: "Strife and contention are the primary teaching; indolence is the secondary practice. This is the ultimate word of the ancient sages, verified this very day.
With his whisk, he drew a single line. Since the mud-vajra does not sweat, how could the stone tortoise ever have understood speech?
He ascended the hall and said: "I cite Chan Master Deshuo Hepan, whose reputation was great at the lecture halls; the two rivers hailed him as a 'Tiger of Doctrine.'"
A visiting monk first visited Huanglong and asked: "When Ānanda questioned Kāśyapa, 'Aside from the transmission of the golden robe by the World-Honored One, what else was transmitted?
Kāśyapa replied, 'Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate. What is the meaning of this? Huanglong said:
"Have you, Master, ever been to Yuzan while traveling through Shu? The monk said: "I have. Huanglong said: "Did you ever stay there as a guest? The monk said: "I did."
One night, he suddenly had an awakening. Long said, "Zhizhe’s Dharma site has General Guan; why would it be improper to offer incense and establish a karmic connection with him?
For a long while, Shanshan remained silent, then repeated his previous question. Huanglong lowered his head, whereupon Shanshan hurried out and attained a sudden, clear realization.

Startled greatly, he said, "The tiger of righteousness from the Two Rivers need not endure even a single spittle from this old man. The Master said, "The tiger of righteousness inquires again, yet does not deceive himself;
Huanglong bows his head, which only increases people's doubts. Take up the Vajra-pestle of daily life and you shall shatter the iron staff of many years. *Du!* (Hush!)"
Opening the Guest Quarters for the Assembly. According to the ancient customs of the monastic groves, it is only on the first day of the eighth month that the guest quarters are opened.

This was intended for the sake of Zen practitioners from all quarters who, having spent the summer retreat here, pass the winter there, seeking out friends and teachers to resolve the great matter of their own being.
Nowadays, however, it is not so; there is neither summer nor winter. One stays if one wishes to stay, and leaves if one wishes to leave. Suddenly—
Nevertheless, he ran off to a desolate village and an ancient monastery to seek food. There he encountered an old, withered fellow whose nose was dripping down his chin.
When the man asked, "Venerable sir, you have come from the great quarters; what is this matter of your own person?
he was so lightly questioned that his eyes became like drum-sticks and his mouth like a wooden pestle. Instead of gaining insight, he gave rise to heterodox views and increased his ignorance.

Thus it is said: "The karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no foundation to rely upon. This refers to those very monks who are called "those who have emerged from the groves and entered the monastic community.
On a future day, when the Old Man Yama demands the payment for his meal, there will be something to say.
As for this assembly of mine, there is no need for further elaboration. With the heat subsiding and the coolness arising, I humbly entreat you all to take care of yourselves.
Ascending the hall on the Mid-Autumn Festival: "In greedily gazing at the moon in the sky, one loses the lamp within the room.
How thick is the skin of the ancient worthy who speaks thus? [The Master] suddenly grasps the staff and strikes once.
"There is a reason, yet no basis for it. The waist-dropping stone in Huangmei Mountain; the record of Old Lu in the first year of the Longshuo era."
Ascending the hall: Having been ill for a long time, I have only just risen. Striking the drum, I ascend the hall; my mouth and tongue are dull and heavy, and there is nothing to be proclaimed.
The newly appointed Librarian is a man of high standing from the land of Japan. As the attendant burns incense and makes his inquiries, one does not yet know where he will find his footing.
"The superior man (Shang Daren), Qiu Yiji—transforming three thousand seventy scholars, they shall know the rites. [He] strikes the whisk and descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall on the ninth day: Today is the ninth day of the ninth month. Who does not know this? A cup of *zhuyu* (callicarpa) tea—its wine may be purchased from others.
A true patch-robed monk of the Five Lakes dies before the mind has even been raised. Tianning makes this announcement in such a manner.
"This is indeed the true reality. (He strikes the whisk. "When there is spirit, add more spirit; where there is no elegance, there is elegance nonetheless.
He ascends the hall and cites Master Shending Yin’s citation of Nanquan’s saying: "At eighteen, I already understood how to live."
Ji said, "Zhaozhou said, 'At eighteen, I already knew how to break up the family and scatter the household.

Shending asked, 'Tell me, is it better to break up the family and scatter the household, or is it better to understand how to manage one's livelihood? For a person at the beginning of their practice, they should follow the former words;

however, for those who have long been in the training and are veteran practitioners, they must truly break up the family and scatter the household—furthermore, it is like being sent ten thousand *li* away to Yezhou. The Master said, "There is."

This is the Way. Master Shending’s methods of granting and revoking are worth observing; his restraint and encouragement follow a standard. Little do they realize that he has wrongly applied names and phrases.

Under the gate of Tianning, those who understand how to make a living should receive twenty blows; as for those who destroy their homes and disperse their households—[they too should receive twenty blows].
I would give him twenty blows. Have you not heard it said: "Regulate them with ritual"?
The furnace is opened; I ascend the hall. Today is the first day of the tenth month. Throughout all the monasteries, the furnaces have been opened.
Yet in this ancient temple of ours, the city wall, we are unfortunate to have no firewood or charcoal at all. Venerable Ānanda is left utterly embarrassed; he flees and hides behind a pillar.
He went inside. At the mountain gate, the Vajra Deity joined his palms in praise, saying: "What a fine tradition of the ancient Buddhas!
It truly transcends emotion and is beyond all description. Suddenly, he took up his staff and struck it once, saying: "Those who know this—after them, who else shall know?"

Incense Offering for the Anniversary of the Patriarch’s Death: Crossing sands and deserts, traveling through Wei and visiting Liang, he sat facing the wall for nine years; thus were skin and marrow distinguished.
Striking the incense burner with the incense, he says: "The talk of calamities befalling the monastic community grows ever longer."

The donor arrived, and the Abbot and Chief Administrator offered their thanks; they ascended the hall. "The twenty-five realms of existence within the three worlds arise from the dust of worldly toil.
Among the gates of the six *pāramitās*, giving is supreme. This is clearly stated throughout the entire Great Canon of Teachings. [The Master] raised his staff:
"As for the 'chestnut thorn' of Yangqi, one must strictly avoid swallowing it whole."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The physical body composed of the four great elements does not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma. The liver, gallbladder, spleen, and stomach do not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma.
Empty space does not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma. Only that which is within each person—vividly and singularly luminous—[understands]."
"To explain the Dharma and listen to the Dharma—ancients spoke thus, suppressing their majestic brilliance by how much! Tianning, however, does not do so;
he strikes the whisk and descends from his seat."
On the Winter Solstice, he ascended the hall. He cited Master Guishan’s address to the assembly, which said: "The bitter cold of mid-winter is an annual affair;
as the movement of the sun’s shadow shifts, what is the matter? Yangshan stepped forward and stood with his hands clasped.
Guishan said, "I know well that you cannot answer this question. He then asked Xiangyan, who replied, "I am uniquely able to answer this question. Guishan—
He asked Xiangyan again. Xiangyan also stepped forward, stood with his hands clasped, and remained silent. Guishan said, "Fortunately, you, Jizi, do not understand.
The Master [Zhaozhou] said, "Some say that since the questions were similar and the answers were likewise the same, why did he accept one and reject the other?

Little do they realize that this is the家风 (family style) of the Guiyang and Linji houses: though father and son are close, when the conversation reaches a point of ambiguity, they remain as if separated by a vast distance."
The sea exists; why must Heaven necessarily sever what is uneven? [The Master] brandishes his staff and strikes once. He ascends the hall.
A monk asks, "What is the pivotal bolt of the ultimate? The Master says, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor.
The monk steps forward and says, "Green mountains shroud white clouds; travelers have never reached them. The Master says, "The horse is lean, yet its mane is long. The monk bows.
The Master gave a shout and then said: "Words cannot fully express the matter; speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish;
those who linger in phrases are deluded. He took up his staff and said: "From South India to North Wutai, all are atop this mountain monk’s staff."
The Master of the Hall: Rain falls and the steps are wet; when the sky clears, there is no more mud.
When the Buddha attained enlightenment, he ascended the hall and said: "What was accomplished during six years in the Snowy Mountains? In the midnight void, one beholds the morning star;
The golden crow and jade hare rise and fall. How many people's eyes have been changed?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Shuilao asking Mazu about the "exact meaning of coming from the West. Mazu kicked him in the chest, knocking him down.
Suddenly, Shuilao attained realization; rising up, he clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying, "How marvelous!
How marvelous! Hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings—I have recognized them all at once upon the tip of a single hair!"
He departed from the source, prostrated, and withdrew. The Master said, "Throughout the monastic communities, everyone says that Shuilao was trampled down by Mazu and thereby attained an awakening.
Little do they realize that it was actually Mazu who was thoroughly smeared by Shuilao at that time."
To this day, there is no place to escape shame. [The Master] picks up his staff and says: "A thousand-year field has eight hundred owners.

He strikes the ground with the staff and says: "On New Year's Eve, a small *xuan* (sermon). If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season.

When the time and season arrive, its principle will manifest of itself. Have you not seen how a monk asked an ancient worthy, "When the year ends and the age is exhausted, what then? The ancient worthy said, "East..."
The village king burns paper money at night. Regarding this saying, those in the monastic communities mostly produce interpretations based on the literal words;
fortunately, there is no connection here. Consider, for instance, when a monk asked Master Yangqi, "What is the Buddha?
Yangqi replied, "A three-legged donkey prances about on its hooves. How would you deliberate upon this? Even if one were to say that gold is not traded for gold, or water for water...
"Not washing at a waterless place"—this path is attained with such lofty clarity that it is like a cloth for wiping bowls in the kitchen.
Suddenly seizing his staff, he struck once: "A thousand-person tent in the north of the steppes; ten-thousand-hu of a boat in the south of the Yangtze.

He then spoke a verse: "The reed-arrows of the Five Indias stir up China; When snow melts and ice withers, what shall become of affairs? After tomorrow, when the three yangs meet in harmony, [all shall be resolved]."
It is fitting to join in singing the Song of Great Peace.

On the occasion of ascending the hall for the New Year: as the first month of the year begins its auspicious reign and the phoenix calendar is renewed, the drum is struck and we ascend the hall—what matter should we discuss together?
Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; a sovereign attains the One and achieves civil brilliance and supreme governance;
a patch-robed monk attains the One and his nostrils reach to the heavens. (He raises his staff. Tell me, when this staff attains the One, what exactly is so extraordinary about it?
(With the staff, he draws a line. He cuts off the waters of the Jing River and parts the clouds of Mount Mao.

Addressing the assembly: Monasteries everywhere are now desolate; the Dharma of the Final Age shall last ten thousand years. Most practitioners harbor their livelihoods within ghost caves of mere intellectual knowledge;
who can wield the Dragon Spring sword with full majesty? Since the tiger has already been subdued, there is no need to sit; while the slumbering serpent has not yet emerged, how can one sleep?
A single phrase that strikes the vital point spreads throughout the universe: beneath the mountain of Staff Grove lies the bamboo-tendon whip.
Ascending the hall on the Lantern Festival: One, two, three, four, five—the people of Silla and Campā compete for the forehead mark.
Four, five, three, two, one—the lanterns and the pillar intersect. [With his whisk, he draws a line: The frog at the bottom of the well swallows the moon;
the silent youth speaks with a babbling mouth.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring mountains layer upon layer in wild green; the spring waters shimmer in empty azure.
Vast and silent between heaven and earth, standing alone, what limit can one’s gaze reach? Some say that Master Xuedou, out of his great compassion, spoke these words as if descending into the weeds.
Tianning cannot help but provide a commentary from the very beginning: "The spring mountains layer upon layer in wild green"—when a guest arrives, you must look! "The spring waters..."
The vast void is azure. When a thief comes, one must strike him. Throughout the vastness of heaven and earth, there is no "real" asafoetida; standing alone, what limit can one's gaze reach?
There is no "false" mercury. [The Master] strikes the whisk and descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall at the beginning of the summer retreat: Mañjuśrī spent the summer in three places; Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years.
But tell me, what was the intent behind this? (With the whisk, he draws a line.

If you can see it here, you could transform the great earth into gold and churn the long river into butter and milk to offer to the Elder—this would not be considered going beyond your bounds. If you have not yet realized this, then simply prepare yourself for this entire summer.
Investigate and seek it out; wait until the autumn wind blows, then ask for the ford.

Entering the hall: Setting aside for a moment the hair swallowing the vast ocean and the mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru, [consider] the Tathāgata King of a Thousand Radiances Abiding in Tranquility.
Upon the tip of the whisk at Tianning Monastery, the ninety-day summer retreat has already passed its halfway mark. Now tell me:
how can one say that "merit is not bestowed in vain"? Ultimately, how should this be proclaimed? After a long silence, his breath was like a bellows—something truly admirable.
Ascending the hall, he raised an ancient precedent, saying: "The Buddha is born from non-reliance. If you awaken to non-reliance, even the Buddha cannot be found.
The Buddha is born from non-reliance; wherever you strike or bump against him, if you awaken to non-reliance, even the Buddha cannot be found.
Where have the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics gone? He drew a line with his whisk. Qingyuan—
Three cups of wine at the White House; having drunk them, one still says the lips have not been moistened.
[The Master] ascends the hall and cites a monk’s question to Chan Master Benren of Baishui: “What is the meaning of ‘non-transmigration’? Ren replied: “Falling flowers follow the flowing water;
the bright moon ascends the high peak. The Master said: “Excellent indeed is the meaning of non-transmigration! Baishui has exerted his full strength.”
He could only express it as eighty percent. When asked, "What is the meaning of 'non-transmigration'? Tianning simply replied:
"A colorful phoenix dances in the crimson heavens; a tortoise drills through a broken wall."
Ascending the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat: How many times have mulberry fields turned to sea and withered away? Last night the western wind reached the well-side catalpas.
Amidst the vast expanse of dust, one must discern the master; Śākyamuni and Maitreya are but his servants.
Ascending the hall, he raised the teaching: "Abiding at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts. Sand cannot enter the eyes;
yet, as for these various deluded minds, one does not suppress or extinguish them. Water cannot enter the ears; one dwells within the realm of false conceptions without adding further discernment.
A frog leaps up to the Brahma Heaven; lacking discernment, one fails to distinguish the truth. An earthworm passes straight through.
The Eastern Sea. [He] raises his staff. "Śākyamuni Buddha is coming! [He] plants the staff down. "There are no overnight guests at the Dragon Gate;
turtles and cranes naturally become immortals."
Addressing the assembly: Burying one’s head amidst words of profound mystery, how many can pass the barrier with arms akimbo? The waves and storms of the dream-state are empty and perilous;
the sun and moon of the awakened heaven are fundamentally vast and leisurely. Dingguang beckoned from afar at Golden Mountain; Kāśyapa alone broke into a smile on Vulture Peak.
I wish to re-examine this from the beginning, lest you continue forever to peer through a tube for a mere glimpse of the whole.
Double Ninth. A formal address upon ascending the hall to thank Prime Minister Xie for providing the funds to repair the Buddha Hall, and to thank the West Hall Monitor for overseeing the harvest.
He is a pillar of the imperial house and a golden bulwark for the Buddha-Dharma; he is truly a man of great power. When the rice ripens in the fields, it must be harvested in due time;
when every grain is fully formed, there is no need to seek elsewhere. This is the very application of a monk. Now tell me: Mañjuśrī is the [wisdom] of the seven Buddhas—what is his function?
The Master said, "For what reason were you listening to the Dharma under Śākyamuni? He then drew a line with his whisk. "Three years meet once at the intercalary month;
the ninth day is the Double Ninth Festival."
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: Master Nanchan Luohan addressed the assembly, saying: "Red clouds pierce the azure void; White egrets dot the vast marsh.
Were it not for Hanshan, Who would come to this ancient ferryhead? Riding a fine steed, galloping atop a high tower, The ten-thousand-mile Milky Way rolls like a jade ball.
Seeking a separate, true liberation, One stirs the fire to search for floating bubbles. He then composed a verse himself to illustrate this: [Verse follows]
O Great Assembly! Directly beneath the Azure Dragon Cave, he kicks over Parrot Isle. When the Persian enters the bustling marketplace, how many do not turn their heads?
Striking the iron drum at the Sleeping Dragon Tower, an eighty-year-old rolls the embroidered ball. His mother-born eyes are alive and alert.
"Do not mistake the ocean for a bubble. [He] struck the whisk and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The single moon universally appears in all waters; the moon in all waters is encompassed by the single moon.
Master Yongjia exhausted his spiritual powers, yet he could only express half of it. [The Master] took up the staff: "When an object meets its master, the eye stands upright. *Fengxi*.
"Not dwelling in the *wutong* tree.
[This was said when] he retired from the monastery and ascended the hall. An ancient worthy said: "When staying, the solitary crane perches coldly atop the pine summit;

when departing, a single fragment of cloud suddenly passes through the human world. Tianning, however, says it is not so: "If you recognize your own Avalokiteśvara, then in every speck of dust and every world-system [it is present]."
Compiled by his disciples Wenwei and Yundan, et al.,
from the *Recorded Sayings* of [Master] Touxian at Tiantong Chan Monastery.
The Master entered the temple and, pointing to the mountain gate, said: "Layer upon layer, the inexhaustible Flower Treasury Sea; layer upon layer, the inexhaustible gates of the pavilions.
Without even the need to snap one's fingers, one transcends directly and enters."
Buddha Hall. Incense Offering: “The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories. A stone ox blocks the ancient road; one horse gives birth to three tigers.
Ancestral Hall: “Iron jaws and copper heads; donkey cheeks and horse jaws. If you claim to transmit the mind-seal of the Buddhas, each and every one of you must undergo this [examination] again.”

Relying on the chamber, he grasps the master’s staff. This is the law of Magadha, the true rule of Shaoshi. To hold fast, the silt and sand conceal their luster;
to let go, the blazing fire radiates its light. He leans upon the staff.

A Brief Commentary: The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates are all sealed by a single seal. Great achievement remains unassuming; the vast expanse has no exterior. This monastery’s memorial states:
To erect the banner of the Dharma and establish the fundamental tenets, so that the elephants and dragons of the four seas shall become the peaches and plums of a single house.

Commentary on the Various Mountains: Each possesses its own great eye; each supports and upholds the vehicle of the school. In the sixth month, the Yellow River freezes through to its depths. Commentary on the Rivers and Lakes:
From earth to north and heaven to south, the nets are gathered and the hooks laid aside. Dragons and elephants trample over it; it is not something a donkey can endure.
Pointing to the seat, he said, "This seat is high and broad; I cannot ascend it. Speaking thus, he did not deceive Xintiantong. Thereupon, he ascended the seat with rapid strides.
Having offered incense and made his vow for the Emperor, he adjusted his robes and took his place.
The head monk struck the gavel and declared: "O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast, you should contemplate the foremost [truth]."

Yi asked, "Our school has no words or phrases, nor do we bestow a single dharma upon others. We have opened a 'thread of light' for those who might engage in discussion. Is there anyone here who has utterly transcended the sense-bases and their objects, and stands alone beyond words and images? A monk asked, "The nine ridges stand firm amidst the sky; the twin ponds shimmer with empty azure. This is far superior to the ancient site of enlightenment, where ten thousand fingers dwell together in repose. How fortunate to encounter this! [The Master] said: "For what purpose have you come? The monk replied, "I have come seeking the Way. The Master said, "The Way cannot be sought. If you seek it, you will lose it. Do not seek it within the mind, nor seek it outside the mind. Do not seek it within the senses, nor seek it outside the senses. Do not seek it within the body, nor seek it outside the body. Do not seek it within the world, nor seek it outside the world. It is right here before your very eyes. Since you have come seeking, you have already lost it. The monk asked, "If one does not seek it, how can one attain it? The Master said, "Attainment is itself loss. If you wish to attain it, you must first abandon all seeking. Once seeking is abandoned, you will naturally find it. The monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "The Way is not a thing that can be grasped. It is like the vast sky—how could it be measured? It is like the great ocean—how could it be fathomed? It is like a great mountain—how could it be climbed? It is like a great river—how could it be crossed? It is like the sun and moon—how could they be grasped? It is like the four seasons—how could they be constrained? It is like the myriad phenomena—how could they be exhausted? It is like the ten thousand things—how could they be numbered? It is like the great earth—how could it be moved? It is like the great void—how could it be filled? It is like the great fire—how could it be extinguished? It is like the great wind—how could it be stopped? It is like the great thunder—how could it be heard? It is like the great rain—how could it be caught? An iron ox has no fear of the lion’s roar.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return?
Zhaozhou said, "When I was in Qingzhou, I made a robe of plain cloth that weighed seven jin."
All phenomena return to the One; to what does the One return? Who will fit a round log into a square hole?
When Zhaozhou was in Qingzhou, he made a cotton robe weighing seven catties.
When Mazu Daishi was unwell, the head of the monastery asked him, "How has your health been lately, Reverend?
The Master replied, "The Buddha of the Sun’s Face, the Buddha of the Moon’s Face."
When the head of the monastery asks, it is naturally easy; when the Great Master answers, it is likewise not difficult. This single song on the stringless zither is uniquely natural;
from the earth to the heavens, who can play it?
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Dharma-body? Yunmen said, "Not contained within the six. Regarding Yunmen’s "not contained within the six":
the Earth-Roaming Star rides a cow backward; he kicks over the four great oceans and ascends straight to the Five-Cloud Pavilion.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is Zhaozhou? Zhaozhou replied, "The east gate, the west gate, the south gate, and the north gate.
Crows fly and rabbits run; at dawn it is bright, and by evening it is dusk. Zhaozhou is the Tathāgata’s recognition of the gates of the four directions."
Whenever Master Juezhì was asked anything, he would simply raise one finger. Raise one finger!
Old Juezhì—lightning is not swift enough for him, and sparks from flint are still too slow. From the beginning, there has never been much to this Buddha-dharma;
it is permitted only for the black cat and the white ox to know it.
A monk asked Xianglin, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Xianglin said, "Sitting for long becomes weary.
Under the gate of the patch-robed monks, there is no need for much talk; the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West is simply that sitting for long becomes weary.
A monk asked Baizhang, "What is the extraordinary matter? Baizhang said, "Sitting alone on Mount Daxiong.
The monk bowed; Baizhang then struck him.
When someone asks about a marvelous matter, he simply says, "I sit alone on Mount Daxiong. He waits for them to prostrate, then strikes them across the spine;
this is like a Persian reciting the Eightfold Repentance.
Eulogies for the Venerable Liaotang by His Disciples Zongyuan, Silian, and Others; Compiled by Zongyuan and Silian.
Amitābha Buddha.
I prostrate to the Great Teacher of the Land of Bliss. For vast eons, you have mounted the wheel of this great vow;

like the bright sun rising in the void, sentient beings receive its benefit without end. You expound the subtle and wondrous Supreme Vehicle; your tongue’s manifestation covers the entire trichiliocosm.
Sentient beings, long lost in delusion and wandering astray, you widely open for them the gates of skillful means for their gathering and guidance. With a single heart of sincere devotion—
Second is the profound mind (*adhyāśaya-citta*). Third is the mind of dedication and aspiration (*pariṇāmanā-praṇidhāna-citta*).

When the karma of worldly toil has ceased in Jambudvīpa, those of the nine grades shall all be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*). Seven layers of trees tower high, providing every kind of joy; layer upon layer, jeweled nets interlace with light.
Flowers of four colors bloom in ponds of eight virtues (*aṣṭāṅga-guṇa-toya*); the fragrant water within these ponds is ever full. White cranes, peacocks, parrots, and other [birds...]

From their mouths, they simultaneously utter harmonious and elegant sounds; as subject and object mutually merge, they proclaim the Dharma-transformation. This is truly not born of the retribution of sin; the merit of the Guide is inconceivable.
To describe it, I would say one holds a measuring rod to measure empty space; the excellence of the Land of Bliss is inconceivable.

To describe it, I would say one holds a conch shell to fathom the vast ocean. To see through to the fundamental nature is to be Amitābha himself; to understand clearly that it is but the mind itself—this is the ultimate truth.
The Pure Land. The oceans of lands in the ten directions are all sealed and brought to rest; the Tathāgatas of the ten directions equally bear witness.
When I contemplate the emergence of the ancient sages, there is nothing that is not through inconceivable power. When the Layman Vimalakīrti manifested illness at Vaiśālī, it was especially so.

The wisdom of the world cannot fathom it. Borrowing a jeweled throne from the Lamp-King Buddha and requesting alms-food from the Fragrant Accumulation Buddha, he placed the land of Wondrous Joy upon the tip of a needle as easily as setting a jujube on a leaf.
In disparaging the partial and striking down the small, his gaze was fixed toward the southeast; in praising the Great and extolling the Perfect, his intent lay toward the northwest.
May you now extend even a hair’s breadth of your supernatural powers to instantly dispel the delusions of all sentient beings. Since it has been said:
The nature of words is emptiness. Why did you, Mañjuśrī, respond with silence?
Great Being Samantabhadra, I prostrate to the Great Being Samantabhadra, whose great conduct and great vows deliver sentient beings throughout every single atom of the boundless Dharma-realm.

They enter everywhere into the midst of atoms. Within every atom are jewel-adorned lands, and in each land there is a Great Being holding a volume of the sublime Lotus Sutra, sitting upright upon a snow-white elephant king.
When sentient beings achieve a single moment of resonance with this thought, the Great Being immediately appears before them.
As long as the ocean of karma of sentient beings is not emptied, the practices and vows of the Great Being shall never end.
Taking the empty space of the ten directions for a mouth and the billion Sumeru mountains for tongues, one extols the virtues of the Great Being. How can these virtues be extolled?

The Great Being Avalokiteśvara observes that the multitudes of beings within the three realms are themselves ignorant of their own numinous spirit; their vision does not transcend form, and their hearing does not extend beyond sound.

The Great Being manifests his vision through manifold skillful means: when he sits in tranquil meditation contemplating emptiness, what is there to be seen in emptiness? Yet when drums are struck throughout the ten directions, his hearing is nowhere not perfect.
Bondage and liberation are non-dual. The faculties and their objects share a common source. True compassion is not compassion; true teaching is without words.

Ten thousand lands experience the spring, and a thousand rivers reflect the moon. The fourteen fearlessnesses are fully manifested in every land; the four immeasurable minds universally respond in every particle of dust.
How often have sentient beings been deluded regarding the realm of beings? Yet they insist that the ear-faculty is the proof of perfect penetration.

The void can be measured; even an iron wall can be entered. The Great Being’s manifestation is beyond the reach of words and thought; whether through meditative concentration or wisdom, it is ineffable.
Whether through compassion or majesty, he does not violate his original vow; he universally responds to the capacities of all beings.

A prayer-bead in his hand, a lotus beneath his feet, the bright moon at the edge of the sky, the reflection of heaven in the water—his compassionate vow to deliver sentient beings is naturally inexhaustible.
Which sentient being has not yet perfected their awakening?

The entire body is this sutra; though one has a mouth, it cannot be spoken. It grandly opens the gate of perfect penetration. Sitting upright upon the pāṇḍaka stone, the Great Being’s sutra-text is neither identical nor separate.
Emptiness and awakening are utterly perfect; they are neither the same nor different. Upon the tip of a single hair, perfect penetration is revealed:
at midnight, the golden sun glows red from the bottom of the sea.
With jade-like features and cloud-like tresses, her beauty is surpassed by none; she displays true compassion within the realm of Jambudvīpa.
Amidst the vast, surging red dust where people are like the sea, to whom shall she sell the golden scales from her basket?
Master Bāguǐ and President Chiang pursue this idle, simple monk; where on his back has there ever been an eye?
All say that Chángtīng produced Maitreya, yet to this day flowing water cannot wash away the stain.

Patting people on their backs to seek a single coin, he runs through the streets carrying a bamboo pole. On the occasion of the Dragon Flower Assembly, this Honored One of the Successor’s Seat puts forth all manner of wretched antics.
Not existing before the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvara, nor falling behind Kāśyapa; having opened the sack of tattered rags, everything is found within.
The nostrils are clearly missing half their span, yet even a sneeze becomes the lion’s roar.

The Great Being Zhenjue of Jinling wore tattered robes, went barefoot, and let his hair fall to his shoulders. Who would say that Lu Tanwei’s painting was incomplete? There is another extraordinary feature shown to people:
a pair of scissors, a mirror, and a ruler are suspended from the head of his staff.
The fragrance of the precepts fills the silent woman;

the long corridor gives birth to the broom that sweeps away dust. Having come through vast eons with the profound vehicle of compassionate vows, she has filled the entire world by inheriting words and phrases.
Thus, she opens her mute mouth toward all people.
The gilded Arhats crossing the water emerge from the ocean-store of Vairocana.
They are profoundly still and eternally tranquil; yet, when a single thought flickers, their ascent and descent become boundless. Thereupon appeared a holy master.
The ultimate stage of the four fruits, worthy of offerings from the ten directions, who personally received the Buddha’s prophecy;

with a slight display of supernatural powers, traversing the sea and soaring through the air—smoke-staff and rain-cloak, wind-tiger and cloud-dragon—who could take golden pigment to paint these extraordinary forms? Here we pay homage and gaze upon them again and again.
Reaching for the void to pursue an echo:
from the Great Master Bodhidharma down to the Elder Guyuan, there have been twenty-eight generations.
The Tiantai bhikṣu Sisi, the Abbot Tanzang, commissioned artisans to paint individual portraits of each and requested encomiums.

The First Patriarch, Master Bodhidharma, was a "poisonous seed" from the Western Heavens and a "demon" in this Eastern land. His teaching of direct pointing and single transmission became a thousand variations and ten thousand differences.

When he met the King of Liang, he said, "I do not know," thus painting a tiger and ending up with a wildcat. When he encountered Song Yun, he carried a single sandal on his hand, thereby proving a tortoise to be a turtle. The Great Thousandfold World...
The traces of his conduct are cut off throughout the sands of the world. On the high, rounded peak of Mount Xionger, the moon shines;

the Great Master Huikong, the Second Patriarch, gazed toward the True Land (China) as one possessing the vessel for the Mahāyāna. He stood in the snow until it reached his waist and severed his own arm—a man who knew all things clearly and eternally, yet whose words cannot be grasped.
Furthermore: "When the flowers bloom on the iron tree, it does not cease its spring.

The Third Patriarch, Master Can, said, "The offense cannot be found; I have finished repenting for your offenses for you. He then concealed his traces on Mount Huankong. It is the great, impartial, perfect mirror.
The Fourth Patriarch, Master Xinxing, asked:
"Who is binding you that you come seeking liberation? I shall pull the nail from behind your head; you shall live again from within death. Now I am without mind.
How could the Buddhas possibly pluck the Southern Dipper to turn it around or shift the Northern Dipper here?

When the Great Master Wuzu Ren asked for the Dharma, he had no leisure to plant pine trees; yet when he returned at the age of seven, it turned into a mere anecdote. This is the transmission of the ancestors.
An old family heirloom; he had just been demanding a high price from those before him.

The Great Master Huineng of the Sixth Patriarch, having commissioned someone to inscribe [the verse] on the wall, transmitted the robe at midnight. From beginning to end, it was extraordinary; its radiance shone throughout the entire world.

As for Master Nanyue Huairang’s cultivation and realization, they are indeed not non-existent; yet he could not be defiled. When he was grinding a brick to make a mirror, thorns sprouted upon level ground.
Thus it was with Chan Master Mazu Daoyi.

"The very mind is Buddha; neither Buddha nor mind. Reaching for the collar while holding the sleeves, digging into the lapel from under the armpit—only to be pointed out idly by Old Pang, who masterfully plays the single-classed zither without strings.
When Chan Master Baizhang Hai saw a wild duck fly past, he suddenly pulled it back by its nose. "Bo Ya and Ziqi were no ordinary acquaintances.
The next morning, when Mazu ascended the hall, he pointlessly rolled up the ceremonial mats.
Chan Master Huangbo Yun took up a set of alms bowls and sat upon Nanquan’s seat. When someone asked, "When did you begin practicing the Way? he replied, "Before the time of Wei-yin.
Hard as raw iron, soft as cotton; when meeting one who understands, his laughter reaches the heavens.

Chan Master Linji Xuan once took a tumble before Huangbo’s hall; it was only on the Gaoyang rapids that he finally turned over a new leaf. Clearly, he is a master thief who plunders in broad daylight;
beneath the great tree’s cool shade, all people take refuge.
Chan Master Xinghua Jiang humbled Minde and gave a severe beating to Kebin; there was bait on the hook, yet no sinew in his eyes.
Chan Master Nanyuan Yongyong.
I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master. Unfortunately, I encountered the Master of Baoying’s absence. A weary crane seeks the forest; a fierce dragon sports in the sea.

Chan Master Zhao of Fengxue dwells in an ancient temple in the empty mountains; for seven years he has lived alone. He begs for alms from villages to sustain his life, and faces the myriad phenomena while discoursing on Chan.
The orthodox Eye of the True Dharma has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, so that it would not perish with the blind donkey.
Master Shoushan Nian said:
"Kāśyapa heard what cannot be heard; the World-Honored One spoke what cannot be spoken. This is a trivial koan; why labor to make forced distinctions?
How many people possess the clear eye? A single piece of snow upon a red furnace. I grant that Nanfeng thought only of the *Lotus Sūtra*, yet I laugh at old Fengxue.

Chan Master Fenyang Shao’s “acting against the flow” and “acting with the flow” were unfathomable even to Heaven; he made offerings once for the spirits of his parents, and six disciples under his seat attained great realization.
A vessel indeed: the Hu monk requested the Dharma, for his journey was not in vain. Chan Master Ciming Yuan traveled from afar, braving heavy military opposition;
he changed his clothes to resemble those of a latrine attendant. Once the Great Dharma was realized and clarified, his lofty reputation filled the heavens and the earth.
Quandao praised him with the utmost fervor; Yang Dainian wholeheartedly extolled his virtues. Alas!

Chan Master Yangqi Hui’s words gallop like lightning and whirl like a gale, their meaning beyond the literal. Heaven crumbles and earth grows old—who can raise them up? A three-legged donkey prances on its hooves.
Action. A mouthful of frost and ice fills the universe.

When Chan Master Baiyun ended his search for the profound and sought the subtle by parting the weeds and observing the wind, he encountered a "stammering head" (a stubborn, non-conforming type) and burst into a great laugh; there was no door through which to peer.
Do not fall into deliberation. Even if you were to take it up in its entirety, it would still be like calling out into the empty sky.

Chan Master Dongshan Yan’s “Cockcomb Flower” and “Iron Sour Pastry”: add where there is too much, subtract where there is too little. Leaves falling, one knows autumn; opening the mouth, one reveals the gallbladder.
When Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin was just beginning to recover from a fever at Mount Jinshan, and Wuzu Fayan returned to his rightful position, the attendant had already attained enlightenment.
Out of parental affection, he did not wish to let others know.
Chan Master Hongluo of Huqiu possessed the living eye of Mahesvara; his exquisite carving left no trace. His prajñā was profound and his great merit remained unassuming.
His presence in the monastic community was lofty and fresh, while the majestic sleeping tiger retained its full majesty.

Chan Master Ying’an Hua attained the Dharma within the quarters of Mount Huqiu and was entrusted with the robe at Yangyu Hermitage. Looking down upon the stream of Chan practitioners, they flocked to him like clouds and water;
he held aloft the ancestral command, which resounded like thunder and swept like the wind.
Chan Master Miam Jie asked about the "True Dharma Eye," to which he replied, "A broken sand pot. This overawes the Buddhas and Patriarchs and shakes heaven and earth.
— Chan Master Songyuan Yue.
Wielding the vajra-sword, he shatters the net of false teachers' views; employing the method of black beans, he exchanges the eyes of the monks.
Grasping the robe of Yangqi, the essential teaching of Shaolin becomes ever more luminous.
Chan Master Tianmu Li greatly perplexed the fourfold assembly;
he thrice prodded them with "Yellow Teeth. His capacity encompassed the vast ocean, and his faculty was like a precipitous cliff.
He brought forth the bamboo shoots of Nan-shan and the cuttlefish of the Eastern Sea, delighting to test masters within the monastic groves.

Zen Master Hongchuan Gao smoothed away all angularities to achieve perfection, demonstrating the fulfillment of the Way to his disciples. He discarded the flowery to grasp the substantial, taking the Great Dharma upon his own person.
He swept away the corrupt practices of the time and restored the pure customs of antiquity; the myriad phenomena and all living beings turned their eyes in unison toward Mount Mao.
The peak rises high above the Great River to the east.

Chan Master Zhuyuan Dao attained enlightenment in a single morning upon the "dry dung pellet" (gān shǐ jué). His story of the "worn-out straw sandals" has spread throughout the four seas. With this single set of iron-faced skin, he has arrived.
Even unto death he would not change.
Chan Master Fenggan rode a tiger out through the pines; his skillful means for others were extraordinary. Before Governor Lüqiu, his celestial mechanism was entirely revealed.
All leaks have been stopped. Behind the vajra-head is three catties of iron.
The two Great Beings, Hanshan and Shide, are both wind-crazed and madness-crazed; they are neither ordinary nor holy. They cast down the vegetable sieve and let fly the broom handle.
Answering Fenggan’s refusal to visit Wutai, he startled Shishuang as they emerged together onto the pine path. He has written out the hearts of all under heaven through long chants and short odes;

grasping his iron caltrop upside down, he shatters the mirror of Xuanyuan. With a shoulder-pat and a great laugh, he acts with reckless abandon, while the myriad phenomena of the universe rejoice in unison.
Regarding the Venerable Liaohan of Lingyan: his Dharma heir, the Elder Xing of Lizhou, attended him during mountain travels;

half a cup of potent wine was shared like the gall of a river otter, and the divine pearl of the nine bends was threaded through an ant’s silk. On a clear day, he served while they strolled beneath the pines.
The Path. Who says that father and son do not transmit it?
Former Master Guiyuan was once tripped up before the ancient Mount Mofeng; without cause, he stepped upon the head of a dead snake. His descendants are not those who merely boast of their lineage.
"Ugly! The poisonous breath harming people has not yet ceased.
Master Mota Tang, leaning on his staff, has a gaze like a flash of lightning and a countenance as deep and clear as a profound pool.
The assembly of monks bows down like grass before the wind, while the hosts of demons tremble with fear. He is truly like the Great Seven Peaks."
The Five Peaks swell the Western River into the Eastern Sea; this is beyond the measurement of intellectual capacity—how could the True be presented?
Thus I reflect on Puhua’s somersaults: why should Ningxing belong to Panshan alone?
The late Master Yuánmíng of Tiāntóng was the son of Shuāngxī and the grandson of Guīyuán. Like ice withered and snow aged, he continued the flame of their noble lineage.

Within the chamber of Mánfēng, he reviled Buddhas and scolded patriarchs; his realization reached the ultimate subtlety. Upon the summit of Taibáifēng, he coiled dragons and struck phoenixes; his spiritual mechanism penetrated the profound mystery.
The fundamental principles arise from the fallen ground;
a movement stirs the imperial heart in the Nine Heavens. Without relying on the three barriers, one penetrates directly before the time of Wei-yin.
(Self-praise)
The Elder Duan of Mount Tai requested that he personally uphold the lineage from above;
there was never any other instruction. When the tiger roars, the wind arises; when the dragon sighs, the mist rises. In a single snap of the fingers, the eighty thousand gates are perfectly realized;
in a single upturn of the eyes, one has already traveled three thousand li.

The Elder Huifeng Yuan was invited to reside at four different mountain monasteries for thirty years. He thought only of repaying the profound kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. When dawn came, he looked at his reflection upon the clear pond;
every single strand of hair had turned white to its very root.

The Master of Mount Ran requests the transmission of that which is beyond transmission; this is the ancestral style of the Chan cloister. It is the bestowal of that which is beyond bestowal, the fundamental principle for returning to the source.

This is neither a true-bone grandson nor a filial heir who sustains the lineage. Pointing out the tracks of the "wild sheep hanging its horns," one must observe the waves and billows rising upon level ground.

At the invitation of the Elder Dafu Jing, atop Thousand Peaks and at the crossroads of the street, half-deaf and half-dumb, fully releasing and fully gathering, the broken sand-pot rings like gold and strikes like jade;
the dry dung-stick fills the valleys and ditches. The great kindness remains unrepaid, yet my twin hair-tufts have turned to autumn gray. [This was written with] a marvelous brush.
The most difficult place to depict: loving fellow monks while forging enmity.
The junior disciple Jifu requests that Elder Sijing reside in four different mountain hermitages.
A hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses—planting flowers upon stone, grasping at the moon in water. To attempt to depict this would be futile.
The family style is utterly distinct—distinct! The Lion’s teaching of his cubs is the secret of deluding them;

the junior master, Abbot Siqian, treats the Buddhas and Patriarchs as enemies and regards the hordes of demons as his brothers. He haphazardly hurls the golden circle and swallows the chestnut thorn whole.
Picking up a dead snake and making it alive—only then is one a true descendant who has returned to the source.
The Head Seat of the Middle Hall requests:
The patriarch’s kindness is so great it is difficult to repay. Having endured every wind and frost, the head is now white; the year is at its end, the river is empty, and there is nowhere to rest.
In this place, he alone rode his spirited steed up the high tower.
Master Zhuang invited him to smash the sand bowl and sweep away the method of black beans; there was not a shred of authentic lineage to transmit, only empty fists.
Bitterly pungent! Plucking the willow blossoms, plucking the willow blossoms! Alala, alala! My attendant, please speak with a straightforward mind.
With receding gums and white hair, I have ceased my travels across rivers and seas; now, in my old age, I have sought refuge among the misty vines. Baizhang’s Second Visit.
Mazu’s single shout was like a thunderclap in a clear sky; the National Teacher’s three calls and the attendant’s three responses were like wind and waves on level ground.
These stories have long been current throughout the monastic communities, yet there are still many monks who misunderstand them. Do not attempt to depict me with a piece of raw silk;
lift your eyes and the hawk has already flown to Silla.

Master Wei, Master of the Repository, requests treatment for his hunger—why need one roast the marrow of a phoenix? To mend the broken string, one must naturally take up the dragon’s sinew. The robe of Huangmei was entrusted to a guest who carried the mortar;
though seven hundred men heard of his wondrous understanding, it was all in vain.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Liaotang, Volume Two;
The Recorded Sayings of Master Liaotang, Volume Three;
Verses and Hymns of Master Liaotang.
Compiled by the disciples Wendu, Wenlang, and others, this verse in rhyme is presented to the Abbot Shu upon his second visit to Master Liaohan of Lingyan:
The *maṇi* jewel turns of its own accord; To cast it aside is near, yet to grasp it is far. From the bottom of the great ocean, motes of dust arise.
Great waves surge atop the summit of Mount Sumeru; it is neither mind nor Buddha. From the crown of the head, a falcon from the vast heavens is released.
The clouds clear from the long sky as the moon shines at the third watch; holding an iron pestle upside down, one strikes the icy bones.
Since the secret meaning is already clear within oneself, why need one buy a boat for the Three Wu regions again? Old Man Lingyan is far too talkative; let his command be carried out—strike!
Three hundred lashes.
*Song of Linghe*. Following the rhyme of Master Wuyan:
"Linghe, Linghe, I sing for you: without wind, waves rise to the heavens; turning my head, I already perceive the vast blue sea."
Narrow! How can the myriad streams flow toward the sea like this? With a source so distant, the current comes from Mahāgama; silver mountains and iron walls are all penetrated.
In the sixth month, when yin arises, the gathering of fires grows cool; in the three winters, when flames burst forth, the ice-river becomes hot.

Spirit-like, it is neither within nor without; from antiquity to the present, there is no lingering or waiting. When the song ends under the bright moon, the night hall is empty; the celestial wind shakes—
Moving the thousand-year-old cypress trees.

Following the rhyme of the ancient Master Ding of Zhongzhu, I present this to the Chan Master Yun as he unfolds his Buddha-hand and extends his donkey-feet; where the lamp-stand and the lantern strike and clash, it is specifically for this matter.
Seeking out [the Way], you have come from afar to bestow your instruction; sell away this single pearl within the Tathāgatagarbha. Its numinous radiance is ever-blazing in daily life.
Presented to Head Seat Lang.
Word by word, phrase by phrase, held directly before one’s face—who says it is a secret transmission? When Yongjia reached Caoxi and Shaoyang saw Lingshu, they were true lion cubs;
their spiritual faculties already knew where the point lay. Seven times nine is sixty-three; when meeting people, do not speak of it mistakenly.
The whole earth blooms with five-leaf flowers in spring; the Old Barbarian needlessly crossed the shifting sands himself.

The Great Meaning is called the Superior Man’s Name; it is called the Great Meaning. The Great Meaning is difficult to describe or explain; it is not found in the moment of raising a torch across the river, nor in the place where one opens a field and extends a hand.
Parents are not my kin; the pitch-black Kunlun is pointed out and annotated. The Buddhas are not my...

The Way: The mangy cat climbs upside down upon the Bodhi tree; the ocean of three thousand worlds is fully revealed in every detail, and the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates are manifest at every turn.
Though the Bamboo Mountain has a mouth, it cannot proclaim this; let it be raised up and sent forth to all quarters.
I present to the Abbot of the Repository the Great and Small Tripitakas from Jiangxi to pay homage to the Patriarchs.
Fully raising or partially raising [the teaching], he rides over sounds and covers over forms; he carries water and drags mud. Having ascended Mount Touzi three times, [he has realized the Way].
One night at Caoxi: at dawn, the straw dog barks; at midnight, the wooden rooster crows. Whether in motion or stillness, in cold or warmth, you should cherish yourself.
Where is the Patriarch alone in Jiangxi?
Following the rhyme of Master Wuji, I respond to the Chan practitioner’s inquiry:
Clouds lock the peaks of ten thousand mountains; The mossy path bears no human trace. From where has this pure attendant come? His appearance is ancient, his two pupils are azure.
He himself claims to remember many ancient机缘 (ji-yuan), having traveled everywhere to seek out masters of wisdom. "In my school, there is no dharma to transmit to others;
what benefit is there in this constant exchange of questions and answers? The true gold within his sleeve is not used, while he idly hurls pebbles and rubble about.
Standing before the wind, he cannot help but sigh deeply: "The groves of Prajñā are overgrown with thorns."
Next, following the rhyme of Master Pingshi, I present this in praise of Chan Master Tanchang of Dayun Monastery as he returns from traveling throughout all quarters:
The moss upon the stone bed is emerald green; He has overturned the five thousand scrolls. The six sense-gates are suddenly purified and at ease.
To view others is not right contemplation; non-attainment is true attainment. I am ashamed of myself and repent of my own accord; who could understand this, and who could recognize it?

Whether to employ or set aside [these means] rests with one's own benevolence. The ancient path is as straight as a string; it dries up the ocean of birth and death without requiring the wings of a golden-winged bird.
To the Layman Xubai of Taicheng, who dwells within the lineage of the Western Patriarch:
The direct pointing of the single transmission means that the Sage does not seek elsewhere and the Spirit does not reside within oneself.
Subtle words and wondrous phrases fill the world, yet they are all but useless scraps of paper. Break through the Fenglin Barrier and chop off the yak’s tail.
The old Vimalakīrti within the city of Vaiśālī claps his hands and laughs "he-he" without ceasing.
Following the rhyme of Master Cila-an, I compose this to see off Wood-hermit (Mukan) the Librarian, upon seeing Mr.
Mingqing’s request for a stupa inscription for the Elder Guyuan.
The deep courtyard is empty and profoundly still; I mourn my late teacher with a face clouded by sorrow. Where has the late teacher gone since his passing?
Ten thousand layers of cloudy mountains lock in their cold, azure beauty. Master Muan’s profound silence resounds like thunder, causing my solitary heart to suddenly open.
Holding this verse by my Dharma brother Liaoyan, it is like a bright pearl or white jade, free from even a speck of dust. Since parting from Liaoyan—
As the years have passed again and again, the Great Dharma remains capable of bearing its thousandfold weight. Since Master Huixiu passed away, I have come to the former teacher;
my grief for the Gate of the Lineage is deep, for there is a purpose behind it. Death and life—what are these matters? Waves do not depart from water, and water is itself the waves.

Master Huang is a vessel for the present court and ministry; his source of literary eloquence is vast, overflowing like the Milky Way. I have heard much of his recorded words and accounts of events; his brush—

In his power, he does not fall short of the historian Dong Hu; Liaohan has pointed out Zi-qiu and requested a stele inscription for him. Those with discernment throughout the monastic community all increase their joy, anticipating that one day this shall be engraved upon stone as a magnificent monument.

The "gripping" and "erroneous" phrases are difficult to express in writing; I have always marveled at how the ancient worthies would point to them recklessly with their commentaries—like a donkey looking into a well, or a well looking at a donkey.
Bestowing the *zǎo* cord, he has realized the one and all; once seen, it is not seen again. A frost-sword leaning against the heavens, cold; the parting of ways between killing and giving life.
Xinghua struck Kebin; in the moment, there was little expedient means. Dismissed from the monastery, he was still fined money; when grace is excessive, it turns back into resentment.
If it is great refined gold, its color remains unchanged even after a hundred smeltings. Whether cast away or brought back, how could it ever fail to be seen?
Vast and boundless, people only know how to ask for the capital Chang’an, unaware that they themselves are within the Han-yuan Palace.
Inscription on the Painting of the Realized Man Wang’s Moon-Boat Luminous is the moon in the heavens;
Floating is the boat upon the water. If the moon is obscured by clouds and mist, It is as if the mind is entangled in a hundred sorrows.
A boat may be beset by wind and waves, like a body exhausted by the toil of seeking. One should purify the mind like the moon, serene and soaring through the white autumn sky.

One should take the boat as a metaphor for the body, seeing through existence as something adrift. The moon is fundamentally without light or darkness; the boat simply follows its own coming and going.
I tell you, young disciple Siqui:

to leave home and enter the Way by traveling to various quarters is no small matter. You must succeed to the ancestral school and clarify your own nature. At the age of fifteen, you began your practice of seeking the Dharma;
as you were about to depart, I entrusted you with nothing other than this: do not dally in mountains and waters wasting your precious time, and do not loathe coarse food while envying delicacies.

Sweet and delicious. Do not slight true virtue for the sake of noble empty fame; do not emulate the ignorant by befriending the vulgar and base. In the monasteries of Wu and Chu, those known as "men of knowledge" are many;
morning attendance and evening requests number in the tens of thousands. Staff and shouts fly back and forth like a flash of lightning—here you must directly grasp the meaning prior to words.
"The younger generation is to be feared," says the ancient sage; I am one such who has reached fifty without having heard the Dharma. On another day...
Returning, he resembles Gu Ling; I too shall prepare a fast and offer praise for you.
This is the inscription for the "White Lotus Chamber" of the venerable Ranyu, a white lotus that graces the world.
In Sanskrit, it is called *puṇḍarīka*. Its brilliance and purity are like jade and snow; its fragrance is as rich as agallochum and sandalwood, yet distinct from them.
Observing it, form is not form; smelling it, the nose is not the nose. Thus the ancient sages said: "This Dharma is difficult to conceive.
For those superior persons free from attachment and defilement, they view the world as a phantom dwelling. Taking flowers to name their chamber—this is the true meaning of non-attachment.
Within it, some find peaceful rest; within it, some find playful sport. These flowers and this chamber are neither identical nor separate.
Within the boundless Dharma-realm, who is pure and who is defiled? It is like that great empty space, appearing as flowers born from the cataracts in one's eyes.

Presented to Chan Master Cong upon his journey to Mount Tai and Mount Yan, as a monk came to inquire about his calligraphy: A single word of silence— A golden hook and jade thread cast empty into space. The tabby cat and the white ox sigh in secret;
Shining through antiquity and soaring through the present, what limit can there be? Carrying sun and moon upon his staff, he comes to Tiantai, Climbing its eighteen thousand fathoms.
Lofty and steep! Five hundred śrāvakas have nowhere to be found. The stone bridge and flying waterfalls roar like thunder. Turning abruptly, one might wish to seek out Yandang;
do not spend your efforts on mere sightseeing. Yet even now, you have not yet turned back. When you arrive, it will be well to give a slap across the cheek.
For a monk, the application of means is never difficult: he turns the axis of the earth and revolves the gate of heaven. All together—
Bending and breaking the staff, he smiles as the myriad peaks stir up waves. The Original Nature (Xingyuan) Inscription:
Composed for the sake of the Librarian Zicang on the theme of "Seeing One's Nature and Becoming Buddha;
Buddha is None Other than Nature. The monkey smashes the mirror of Xuanyuan; directly cutting through to the root, nature is not [a thing].
The Original: A turtle sheds its shell and flies up to heaven. "Buddha" is simply "nature"—do not vainly attempt to distinguish them.
"Nature" is not the "Original"—this is even more intimate. A black-lacquered Kunlun dances the *zhazi*; a barefoot Persian chews raw iron.
The practitioner is naturally a dragon among monks; overturning the ocean of the Tripitaka, all must yield to his prowess. The eighty-four thousand afflictions are but a thicket of thorns.

The sun of compassion hangs high; throughout the three hundred and sixty joints and bones, the fragrant breeze spreads universally within the sandalwood forest. Speech and silence are suddenly emptied;

one is utterly liberated from the cage. Thus, even those of a single class who have severed their roots of goodness—the icchantikas—come to know that upon the crown of the heads of the thousand sages lies the orthodox lineage that is not transmitted. *Tu!* (A cry of realization)

I have observed that when a young disciple’s wisdom from traveling to study under various masters surpasses that of their teacher, only then is he fit to receive the transmission. For the most part, they are similar; ultimately, they are not incisive. You are in the prime of your youth.

I hasten toward decline and error. Do not be led astray by fame; do not be enticed by profit. Abandoning sleep at night and forgetting to eat during the day, act as one drowning seeks aid or one burning seeks rescue.
At the gates of all who possess true knowledge, you should everywhere seek counsel and inquiry, as if entering a grove of *campaka* flowers.

He does not smell other fragrances. The ultimate Way is profound and vast; it can ultimately be accomplished. Whether speaking or remaining silent, whether active or in retreat, every aspect remains as it was before.
When he returns in the future, he will be able to withstand insults and reproaches, leaving nothing to shame the ancients—a true scion of our school.

To establish "the profound" (xuan) as "the profound" is certainly not the profound. To establish it—how could one establish it? It is the mother of the myriad transformations; how could it be reached through words or thought?
That it manifests wondrous existence from within absolute emptiness is likewise a deluded attachment of the dust of emotion. Thus, it exhausts heaven and earth and extends...
Past and present: as clear as the sun, as black as lacquer. It cannot be grasped, nor can it be relinquished; yet we forcibly designate it as "the Mysterious Establishment.
Following the rhyme of Master Nantang, I present this verse to the Chan guest Qing.
To open one's mouth is already an error; there is no room for even a fraction [of conceptualization]. To utter a single word is to lose the tradition of our school.

Even if one stands as steep as ten-thousand-fathom cliffs, one must still grind the flour and pound the grain. The World-Honored One pushed aside subtle and minute illnesses of meditation, explicitly naming the five aggregates.

The First Patriarch possessed true and correct knowledge and vision, utterly destroying the six schools. The flowers of the five petals have blossomed in China; the ten-thousand-year-old pine remains.
Zhurong: A wildcat climbs upside down the Bodhi tree; at midnight, the golden sun glows red from the bottom of the sea.
I see off Chan Master Zhang, Custodian of the Tripitaka, as he returns to Kaiyuan Temple to visit his former teacher—the ancient Dharma cave within the city of Suzhou.
There lie two stone Buddhas that drifted from Western India; I hear they have already endured the fires of the kalpa.
The rest remains as it was; the nostrils still stand high and prominent. This man of the Way has come from afar, from Fufou; he probes the profound with a will that marks him no ordinary talent.

Having overturned five thousand scrolls of the scriptural canon, he gazes with a smile upon the two peaks, blue and towering. The Master is old, yet his resolve to return for an audience is most firm;
he does not shrink from the hardships of wind and dust on the long journey. When you arrive, there is no need to present the Perfect Circle; simply stand to one side.
I attend by the corner of the meditation seat. If you should ask about the state of my solitary path: I have contributed nothing to the Dharma lineage, yet my hair has already turned white.
Of the thirty-six thousand acres of Lake Tai, snow-white waves overturn the void and enter my dreams in abundance.
Next, Chan Master Bājiāquán addressed the assembly with this verse:
"The three realms are in turmoil; when will they ever cease? If one traces their origin, there is no cause or condition.

From delusion to further delusion, passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust— We disciples ought naturally to consider turning back. By day we greedily eat, by night we greedily sleep; The rice has not yet been sifted, and the chaff remains."
Winnowing. Skillfully adorning one's speech to manifest one's own virtues, and perversely creating complications to seek out the faults of others—what is appropriate for a jackal?
It is not easy to don the skin of a lion. One’s own fields and gardens lie fallow, yet one is capable of managing all the affairs of another’s household.
Toiling in bitter haste, full of arrogance and conceit, one deeply plants the roots of affliction; how could one ever bear fruit of Bodhi? One day...
A snake has entered his trousers; his soul and gallantry flee—how can he sleep or sit? He cries out, "O Bodhisattva, who will pity me?
I send these thoughts to Master Shangren in the western region.
In your prime, you seek the Way; your resolve must be even firmer. If you have not yet mastered the manner of entering the gate, you must guard against a fist that splits the face.
Whether the novice has a master or not, Zhaozhou once met Nanquan; with a casual hand he plucked it up, and the frozen river burst into flame.
He sat squarely across the path, and the lotus grew upon dry land. If one is a man-eating lion, one must casually penetrate the vanguard of the pivot.
The gateways of the masters are worthy of inquiry: the misty waves of the Three Wu regions meet the distant heavens.
Next, following the rhyme of Master Yian of Baofu, I send off the attendant from Ningbo on his journey to Jinling:
When the sun blazes and the metal melts, it does not heat me; when the glue cracks and the fingers fall off, it does not chill me. A man of spirit exerts his will to surpass the ancients;

plucking the pearl from the dragon’s jaw was never difficult for him. Within the flask, he perceives only the eternal passage of days and months; beyond all measure, one must surely trust in the Way of Heaven.
Kun Kuan. When the World-Honored One held up a flower to show the assembly, only Mahākāśyapa alone broke into a smile.

For two thousand years, this sound like gold and jade has vibrated through both heaven and earth. The spiritual blade and precious sword have always been held in the hand; naturally they shatter the enemy and break through the gates.
Going hence to the base of the ancient city of Jinling, do nothing but pick it up and examine it for me. It is the state of total liberation.
The responsibility rests entirely with you; do not merely keep fiddling with your ball of doubt.

This long song was written at the request of the attendant practitioner, Dao-ren, who sought my calligraphy: "Who can stir a foot of water into a ten-foot wave? Let no original characters remain within the belly."

Feet. You should know that even these literary flourishes are still considered too much. What is the use of composing long songs and writing at length? Smash open the void and seek the seams once more!
If a person, in a single thought-moment, realizes their own error, then in the sixth month the Yellow River will freeze solid to its very bottom.

From the beginning, there has been neither the subtle nor the profound; the myriad phenomena in their dense array cannot be fully grasped. Last night the Southern Dipper shifted toward the north; Ānanda relied [upon it].
Formerly, at the side of the World-Honored One, he sent the Master Fang to travel to Tiantai.

On a day when the sun was high, as Fang was rising from sleep in his moss-covered window, a practitioner produced from his sleeve a scroll of "jade cocoon" paper and said of himself: "For a long time, I have been upon the rivers and seas..."
Wandering, my heart finds no rest before reaching Tiantai. Throughout ancient and modern times, many have traveled there; yet how few can truly fathom its purity and seclusion?
In lofty cliffs and deep valleys, the sound of golden bells resonates; jade fungi and precious herbs drift with celestial fragrances. The Venerable Banzhuan delighted in emptiness and stillness;
sometimes hidden, sometimes manifest, people could not discern him. At times, a tea-flower appeared within his cup; at other times, amidst the pines...

Rooted on mossy stones, the monk’s practice is naturally wondrous. Carrying aloft a seven-foot black staff, if you cannot withstand his every push and shove, be careful not to let him off lightly when the moment arrives.
The Great Plum Record: The Abbot of the Treasury Bakes the Sūtras.
There are great sūtra scrolls that transcend words and speech; both the four sages and the six classes of ordinary beings are thoroughly penetrated by them.

The five hundred cases of the Dragon Palace’s ocean-treasury—needlessly, golden dust settles before one's eyes. Yangqi’s application of the Way is rarely shared by others; if you wish to seek it, look for the hornless antelope hanging from its horns.
The tracks of the sheep: upon the flames of the red furnace, they unfurl and then curl back; the fragrance of ink and flowers turns like mist over the clear sky.

The eyes gaze southeast while the mind dwells on the northwest; when will the silken prize be won? In a single snap of the fingers, the eighty thousand gates are perfectly accomplished—why wait for another life to question Maitreya?
